title: The Personal Best Tracker (Google Doc)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart Jr. describes a classroom self-tracking tool he designed to help students monitor the quantity of their academic work across four domains: words written, texts read, Pop-Up Debate participations, and personal Everest statement commitments. The tracker is grounded in the principle that quality gains in reading, writing, and speaking are often blocked by insufficient quantity, and that making quantity visible is itself a motivation-building intervention for Efficacy specifically — a student who has written thousands of words cannot sincerely claim to be a non-writer. The article also covers Pop-Up Debate floor management through participation floors and optional ceilings, and closes with an invitation for more systematic teachers to improve on the design.
points: Quantifying student output — words written, articles read, debates participated in — is a prerequisite for quality improvement, making tracking not an end in itself but a foundation for deliberate practice.
Students who have produced thousands of words over a semester have concrete self-generated evidence contradicting the anti-Efficacy belief 'I can't write.'
Setting both a floor (everyone speaks once) and an optional ceiling (two speeches per student) in Pop-Up Debates ensures inclusion of the reluctant and manageable space for the eager.
Including the student's Everest statement on the tracker connects the quantitative accounting to a qualitative purpose, preventing the tracking from becoming mere bookkeeping.
The Personal Best Tracker is offered as a starting point for more systematic teachers to improve; its primary value is in establishing a quantity-first orientation toward student growth.
quotes: Sometimes I like to get my students to keep track of the quantity of work they're doing in my class. As I wrote about in These 6 Things, the first step to improvement in an area like reading or writing or speaking is often quantification: what is our current quantity of work?

It's hard to say, 'I can't write' [anti-Efficacy] if you have written thousands of words over the past months. So much of Efficacy development in young people is about proving the student's ability to succeed.

Similarly, I like having my students keep track of the number of textbook pages or articles they've read, and I like to make a big deal about how we read much more in my classroom than the curriculum calls for. When I mini-sermonize on this, I want them to get a sense of pleasure and satisfaction in having done so much reading.

Whenever we do a PUD in my room, the requirement is that everyone participates at least once. If the class is large or has multiple grand-standers in it, I also include a cap on the number of speeches they can give.

I'm sure more organized or systematic teachers will be able to take this simple 'personal best tracker' and make it 100x better and more useful. I'm sharing it for those folks to leapfrog past my practice and enjoy the results.
